title: Protein Structure and Folding
summary: See how a chain of amino acids folds into a precise 3D shape, and what happens when folding fails.

lessons.title: The Peptide Bond and Primary Structure

levels.kid:
Imagine a necklace made of beads. Each bead is a different color, and the order of the colors matters. Proteins are built a lot like that!

The beads are called **amino acids**. There are 20 kinds. Your cells snap them together, one after another, into a long chain. The snap that holds two beads together is called a **peptide bond**. It is very strong, like superglue.

The order of the beads is called the protein's **sequence**. Change just one bead, and the whole protein can work differently. A recipe in your DNA tells your cells exactly which bead comes next.

Later, the chain folds up into a special shape, like a crumpled-up necklace that always crumples the same way.
levels.hs:
Proteins are chains of **amino acids**. Every amino acid has the same core: a central carbon (the **alpha carbon**) attached to an **amino group** (-NH2), a **carboxyl group** (-COOH), a hydrogen, and a **side chain** (the "R group"). The 20 standard side chains differ in size, charge and how much they like water. That is what makes each amino acid unique.

Two amino acids join when the carboxyl group of one reacts with the amino group of the next. A molecule of water is released, so this is a **condensation** (dehydration) reaction. The new C-N link is a **peptide bond**. Breaking it again by adding water is called **hydrolysis**.

A chain of linked amino acids is a **polypeptide**. It has two different ends:
- the **N-terminus**, with a free amino group
- the **C-terminus**, with a free carboxyl group

By convention, sequences are written from N to C, the same direction in which ribosomes build them.

The exact order of amino acids is the protein's **primary structure**. It is encoded by a gene. Primary structure matters enormously. In **sickle cell disease**, one change in the beta chain of hemoglobin, glutamate replaced by valine at position 6, makes hemoglobin molecules stick together when oxygen is low. That bends red blood cells into a sickle shape. One letter out of 146 changes a person's health.
levels.college:
**The peptide bond is not a simple single bond.** The lone pair on the amide nitrogen is delocalized into the carbonyl, so the C-N bond has about 40% double-bond character. Consequences:
- The C-N bond is short (about 1.33 Å, versus about 1.47 Å for a typical C-N single bond).
- Six atoms (Cα, C, O, N, H, Cα) lie in one rigid **peptide plane**.
- Rotation about C-N is restricted. The angle **omega (ω)** is about 180° (**trans**) in nearly all bonds, because cis puts adjacent side chains in steric clash.
- The bond carries a partial dipole (O partial negative, N-H partial positive). This makes the backbone C=O and N-H good hydrogen-bond acceptors and donors.

**Exception: proline.** Its side chain loops back onto the backbone nitrogen, so trans and cis differ less in energy. About 5% of X-Pro bonds are cis in folded proteins, compared with well under 0.1% for other residues.

**Freedom lives in phi and psi.** Rotation occurs around N-Cα (**phi, φ**) and Cα-C (**psi, ψ**). The backbone is a chain of rigid planes hinged at each alpha carbon. These two angles per residue define the backbone conformation.

**Kinetics vs thermodynamics.** Hydrolysis of a peptide bond is thermodynamically favorable in water, yet uncatalyzed it is very slow, with a half-life of hundreds of years at neutral pH. Cells therefore rely on **proteases** to cut proteins, and on the ribosome (powered by GTP and aminoacyl-tRNA activation) to make them.

**Primary structure** is the covalent sequence, including any disulfide bonds (cysteine-cysteine links). It is read N to C and written in three-letter (Gly) or one-letter (G) codes. Sequence determines the side-chain chemistry available for folding, the sites for modification, and evolutionary relationships. Proteins with similar sequences (homologs) usually share structure and function.

**Isoelectric point (pI):** the pH at which a protein's net charge is zero. It depends on the termini plus ionizable side chains, so it follows directly from the sequence.
levels.phd:
**Resonance and planarity, quantified.** The amide's partial double bond gives a rotational barrier around C-N of roughly 15-20 kcal/mol. This explains why cis-trans isomerization is slow, on a seconds-to-minutes scale for prolyl bonds. **Peptidyl-prolyl isomerases** (cyclophilins, FKBPs, parvulins) catalyze it, plausibly by destabilizing the planar ground state. Cyclophilin and FKBP12 are the targets of the immunosuppressants cyclosporin A and tacrolimus (FK506). Inhibition of their isomerase activity is not itself the immunosuppressive mechanism, however. The drug-immunophilin complexes inhibit **calcineurin**. Planarity is also not absolute. ω deviates by ±10° or more in high-resolution structures, and pyramidalization at nitrogen is real.

**Ramachandran (1963)** used hard-sphere steric models to map the allowed (φ, ψ) combinations. The result is the **Ramachandran plot**, now a core validation tool for experimental structures. Glycine, with only an H side chain, reaches regions forbidden to other residues. Proline's ring fixes φ near -65°.

**Sequence determines structure.** **Anfinsen's** experiments on ribonuclease A (Nobel 1972) laid the foundation. He denatured the enzyme with urea and reduced its four disulfides with β-mercaptoethanol, then removed both. Activity recovered, and the native disulfide pairing (one of 105 possible) re-formed. Re-oxidation while urea was still present produced "scrambled" ribonuclease. Activity returned only when trace β-mercaptoethanol allowed disulfide reshuffling. From this came the **thermodynamic hypothesis**: the native state is encoded by the primary sequence under physiological conditions.

**Determining sequence.** Sanger sequenced insulin (Nobel 1958) using N-terminal labeling and overlapping fragments, proving that proteins have defined sequences. **Edman degradation** removes residues one at a time from the N-terminus with phenyl isothiocyanate. Today, **tandem mass spectrometry** dominates. Peptides fragment mainly at amide bonds into b- and y-ions, and their mass ladders spell the sequence.

**Nuance.** "Primary structure" increasingly includes post-translational modifications, which change mass and charge without changing the gene. Some sequences also do not fold alone (intrinsically disordered regions), which complicates a strict one-sequence-one-structure view.
levels.expert:
**Clinical genetics runs on primary structure.** Missense variant interpretation (ACMG/AMP criteria) weighs conservation, the physicochemical distance of the substitution, and the structural context. Glycine-to-anything substitutions in collagen's Gly-X-Y repeat cause **osteogenesis imperfecta**, because only glycine fits inside the triple helix. Substitutions to or from proline often break local backbone geometry.

**AlphaMissense** (2023) predicts pathogenicity for nearly all possible human missense changes. It classified roughly a third as likely pathogenic, but it remains a supporting tool rather than proof.

**Proteomics pitfalls.** Mass-spectrometry identification depends on database matching, so unexpected variants, isoforms or modifications can be missed or misassigned. Leucine and isoleucine are isobaric, meaning they have the same mass, and are hard to tell apart without specialized fragmentation. **De novo sequencing** of antibodies from serum is an active field.

**Pharmacology of the peptide bond.** Peptide drugs suffer protease cleavage and poor oral uptake. Medicinal chemists counter this with D-amino acids, N-methylation (which also favors cis amides and improves membrane permeability, as in cyclosporin), cyclization, and backbone modification. GLP-1 analogues such as **semaglutide** illustrate the approach. An Aib substitution (a non-standard amino acid) resists DPP-4 cleavage, and a fatty-acid chain promotes albumin binding.

**Hydrolysis in the clinic.** Protease inhibitors were designed as **transition-state mimics** of peptide bond hydrolysis. Examples include the HIV protease inhibitors and the ACE inhibitors (ACE is a peptidase). Proteasome inhibitors such as bortezomib, used in myeloma, likewise target the cleavage chemistry.

**Neurosurgical relevance.** Tumor diagnosis now leans on sequence. The **IDH1 R132H** variant (a single residue change) defines a glioma class and is detected with a mutation-specific antibody. The H3 K27M variant defines diffuse midline glioma. **Vorasidenib**, an IDH1/2 inhibitor, was approved in 2024 for grade 2 IDH-mutant glioma.

**Open questions.** How much of the proteome's "dark" sequence space, such as disordered regions and microproteins from small open reading frames, has function? How reliably can sequence-only models predict the effects of variants in disordered regions, where structure-based reasoning fails?

keyPoints: Amino acids share a core (alpha carbon, amino, carboxyl) and differ by side chain
Peptide bonds form by condensation and break by hydrolysis
Resonance makes the peptide bond planar, rigid and usually trans
Backbone flexibility comes from phi and psi rotations
Primary structure is the N-to-C amino acid sequence
Anfinsen showed sequence encodes the folded structure

test.q: Which molecule is released when two amino acids join?
test.explain: Peptide bond formation is a condensation reaction that releases water. Ammonia is not released because the amino nitrogen stays in the bond.

test.q: Why is the peptide bond planar?
choices: Resonance gives C-N partial double-bond character
Disulfide bridges hold the atoms in one plane
Hydrogen bonds between side chains lock it flat
The side chain pins the alpha carbon in place
test.explain: Delocalization of the nitrogen lone pair makes the C-N bond partly double, which restricts rotation.

test.q: Sequences are conventionally written in which direction?
test.explain: Sequences are written N to C, matching the direction ribosomes build the chain.

test.q: In sickle cell disease, hemoglobin's beta chain has:
test.explain: A single substitution at position 6 (Glu to Val) makes hemoglobin aggregate at low oxygen.

test.q: Which residue most often forms cis peptide bonds?
test.explain: Proline's ring narrows the energy gap between cis and trans, so about 5% of X-Pro bonds are cis.

test.q: Backbone flexibility comes mainly from rotation about:
test.explain: Phi (N-Cα) and psi (Cα-C) rotate freely. The C-N bond (omega) is restricted.

test.q: Uncatalyzed peptide hydrolysis in water is:
test.explain: Hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable, but its half-life is hundreds of years. That is why cells need proteases.

test.q: What makes each of the 20 standard amino acids distinct?
test.explain: All share the same core. The R group (side chain) differs.

test.q: The isoelectric point is the pH at which a protein:
test.explain: At the pI, positive and negative charges balance. The pI follows from the sequence.

test.q: What is the reaction called that breaks a peptide bond by adding water?
test.explain: Hydrolysis splits a bond using water, reversing condensation.

test.q: The exact order of amino acids in a protein is its ___ structure.
test.explain: Primary structure is the covalent sequence, read N to C.

test.q: The end of a polypeptide with a free carboxyl group is the ___-terminus.
test.explain: The C-terminus carries the free carboxyl. The N-terminus carries the free amino group.

kidTest.q: What are the 'beads' that make up a protein?
kidTest.explain: Proteins are chains of amino acids.

kidTest.q: How many kinds of amino acid beads are there?
kidTest.explain: There are 20 standard amino acids.

kidTest.q: What happens if you change one bead in the chain?
choices: The protein grows twice as big in size
The whole chain turns into a fat molecule
kidTest.explain: Order matters, so one change can alter how the protein works.

kidTest.q: Where is the recipe for the bead order kept?
kidTest.explain: DNA tells cells which amino acid comes next.

kidTest.q: The bead order is called the protein's s _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: The order of amino acids is the sequence.

advancedTest.q: In Anfinsen's work, re-oxidizing ribonuclease while urea was still present gave scrambled enzyme. Why did trace β-mercaptoethanol rescue activity?
choices: It acted as a chaperone that bound the hydrophobic core
It cleaved peptide bonds and removed the misfolded segments
It converted the cis prolyl bonds directly into trans form
It allowed wrong disulfides to reshuffle toward the native pairing
advancedTest.explain: Disulfide exchange let the protein escape non-native pairings and reach the thermodynamically favored native state.

advancedTest.q: Cyclosporin binds cyclophilin, a prolyl isomerase. What explains its immunosuppression?
choices: Direct hydrolysis of T-cell surface peptides
Blockade of peptide bond formation by ribosomes
Slowed folding of newly made proteins
advancedTest.explain: The immunophilin-drug complex inhibits calcineurin. Loss of isomerase activity is not the mechanism.

advancedTest.q: A peptide drug fails orally and is cleaved rapidly. Which change best addresses both problems?
choices: Raising the backbone's trans amide content
Adding more free N-terminal amino groups
advancedTest.explain: N-methylation and cyclization resist proteases and improve permeability, as cyclosporin shows.

advancedTest.q: Mass spectrometry alone struggles to tell leucine from isoleucine because they:
advancedTest.explain: They are isobaric, so mass ladders cannot separate them without specialized fragmentation.

lessons.title: Secondary Structure: Alpha Helices and Beta Sheets

levels.kid:
Imagine a long string of beads. Each bead is a building block called an amino acid. A protein is a chain of these beads.

The chain does not stay floppy. Parts of it twist into a spiral, like a curly phone cord or a spring. That spiral is called an **alpha helix**.

Other parts lie side by side, back and forth, like folding a paper fan or the strands of a woven mat. That flat shape is a **beta sheet**.

What holds these shapes together? Tiny sticky links called **hydrogen bonds**. Each one is weak, like a single piece of tape. But lots of them together are strong.

Spirals and sheets are the first small shapes a protein makes before it folds into its full shape.
levels.hs:
A protein's **primary structure** is its sequence of amino acids. **Secondary structure** is the next level: regular, repeating shapes that local stretches of the chain fold into.

These shapes are held together by **hydrogen bonds** between atoms of the protein's **backbone**. In the backbone, the C=O (carbonyl) group of one amino acid attracts the N-H group of another. The side chains are not part of these bonds.

The two main types:
- **Alpha helix**: the chain coils into a right-handed spiral. Each C=O bonds to the N-H four amino acids further along, and there are about 3.6 amino acids per turn. The side chains stick outward like bristles on a bottle brush.
- **Beta sheet**: stretched-out segments called **beta strands** line up side by side. Hydrogen bonds form between neighboring strands, making a pleated sheet. Strands can run in the same direction (**parallel**) or opposite directions (**antiparallel**).

Short **turns** and **loops** connect these pieces and let the chain change direction.

A real example: **keratin**, the protein in your hair, is made mostly of long alpha helices twisted together. **Silk fibroin**, made by silkworms, is built mostly from stacked beta sheets, which is part of why silk is strong but not very stretchy.
levels.college:
Secondary structure is the local, regular conformation of the polypeptide backbone, stabilized by backbone-backbone hydrogen bonds.

**Why only certain shapes are possible.** The peptide bond has partial double-bond character, so it is planar and rigid. Rotation can only happen around two bonds per residue: **phi (φ)** (N-Cα) and **psi (ψ)** (Cα-C). Steric clashes forbid most φ/ψ combinations. The **Ramachandran plot** (G. N. Ramachandran, 1963) maps the allowed regions. These regions correspond to the α-helix and β-sheet.

**Alpha helix** (predicted by Linus Pauling, Robert Corey and Herman Branson in 1951):
- Right-handed; 3.6 residues per turn; rise of 1.5 Å per residue; pitch of 5.4 Å.
- Each C=O of residue i hydrogen-bonds to the N-H of residue **i+4**, roughly parallel to the helix axis.
- Side chains point outward. **Amphipathic helices** place hydrophobic residues on one face, which suits packing against a protein core or a membrane.
- **Helix breakers**: **proline** has no backbone N-H and its ring restricts φ. **Glycine** is so flexible that helix formation costs too much entropy. **Alanine, leucine, glutamate and methionine** favor helices.

**Beta sheet**:
- Extended strands (about 3.3-3.5 Å per residue) hydrogen-bond to neighboring strands.
- **Antiparallel** sheets have straighter, more linear hydrogen bonds. **Parallel** sheets have angled ones.
- Side chains alternate above and below the sheet. β-branched residues (**valine, isoleucine, threonine**) and aromatic residues favor strands.
- Sheets usually show a right-handed twist.

**Turns and loops.** **β-turns** reverse chain direction over 4 residues, with an i to i+3 hydrogen bond. They are often rich in Gly and Pro.

**Other helices.** The **3₁₀ helix** (i to i+3) is tighter, and the **π-helix** (i to i+5) is wider. Both are short and less common. The **collagen helix** is a distinct left-handed polyproline II-type helix.
levels.phd:
**Stereochemistry.** The trans peptide unit (ω ≈ 180°) leaves φ and ψ as the backbone degrees of freedom. Ramachandran's hard-sphere analysis placed the right-handed α region near φ ≈ -57°, ψ ≈ -47°. Antiparallel β sits near φ ≈ -139°, ψ ≈ +135°, and parallel β near φ ≈ -119°, ψ ≈ +113°. Glycine populates left-handed (αL) regions forbidden to L-residues. Proline is constrained to φ ≈ -63°. Cis-proline peptide bonds occur in roughly 5% of X-Pro bonds.

**Helix energetics.** Zimm-Bragg and Lifson-Roig theories model the helix-coil transition with two parameters. The first is a **nucleation parameter (σ ≈ 10⁻³)**: the first turn pays a large entropic cost while forming no i/i+4 bonds. The second is a **propagation parameter (s)**. The result is cooperativity: isolated short peptides are rarely helical unless specially designed, such as AK peptides.

The aligned peptide dipoles give the helix a macrodipole. This is often described as about half a unit charge at each end, positive at the N-terminus, although this simple picture is debated. It explains favorable **N-capping** (Ser, Thr, Asp, Asn side chains satisfying free N-H groups), the frequency of anions binding at helix N-termini (e.g., phosphate-binding P-loops), and the C-cap Schellman motif with Gly in αL. Host-guest studies (Baldwin, Scheraga, DeGrado) produced intrinsic helix propensity scales. Alanine is most favorable; proline is about 3 kcal/mol less favorable at internal positions.

**Sheet energetics.** β-propensity depends heavily on context, including cross-strand pairs and tertiary interactions. Sheets can involve residues far apart in sequence, so they cannot be fully understood as local structure. Minimal β-hairpins (e.g., the tryptophan zipper) made sheets tractable to study. Unpaired edge strands are aggregation-prone. Proteins protect them with prolines, charged residues and β-bulges, an idea developed by Richardson and Richardson.

**Context dependence.** Minor and Kim's chameleon sequence experiments showed that an identical 11-residue peptide adopts helix or strand depending on its surroundings. Chou-Fasman and later GOR methods using only local propensities reached about 50-65% accuracy. Profile-based neural networks (PSIPRED) exceeded about 80%.

**Assignment.** DSSP (Kabsch and Sander, 1983) assigns secondary structure from electrostatic hydrogen-bond energies.
levels.expert:
**Measuring secondary structure.** Far-UV **circular dichroism** gives fast estimates. Helices show minima at 222 and 208 nm and a maximum near 192 nm. β-sheets show a single minimum near 216-218 nm. Twisted or aggregated sheets distort these signals, and deconvolution tools such as BeStSel improve sheet estimates. **FTIR** amide I bands are another readout: helix near 1650-1655 cm⁻¹, sheet near 1630 cm⁻¹, and high-frequency antiparallel bands near 1690 cm⁻¹. **NMR chemical shifts** of Cα, Cβ and Hα give residue-level assignments, as in TALOS-N and secondary chemical shift indices. Hydrogen-deuterium exchange MS maps protected, hydrogen-bonded segments.

**Pitfalls.** Trifluoroethanol strongly induces helices, so TFE-stabilized helicity in a peptide may not reflect the native protein. Alpha-helical CD signals can mask minor sheet populations. Static structures underrepresent **fraying** at helix ends.

**Biology and medicine.** Transmembrane helices of about 20 hydrophobic residues span the roughly 30 Å lipid core. Their inserted orientation is predicted by the **positive-inside rule**. These helices define GPCRs, ion channels and transporters, including the S4 voltage-sensor helix with arginine every third position. Many drugs target helix-mediated protein-protein interfaces:
- **Venetoclax** occupies the groove of BCL-2 that normally binds the BH3 helix of pro-apoptotic partners.
- **Hydrocarbon-stapled peptides** (Verdine, Walensky) lock helices in place, improving stability and cell entry.
- Enfuvirtide, a peptide mimicking an HIV gp41 helical region, blocks formation of the six-helix fusion bundle.

Coiled coils, with heptad repeats (abcdefg, hydrophobic a and d), underpin fusion machinery and SNAREs. **β-strand edge pairing** is exploited by some inhibitors and in designing β-strand mimetics.

**Recent advances.** AlphaFold2 (2021) and RoseTTAFold largely solved secondary structure in context. Low pLDDT often flags intrinsically disordered regions. Some of these regions undergo coupled folding and binding, forming a helix only on contact with a partner, as the p53 transactivation domain does with MDM2. De novo design (Baker lab) now builds idealized helical bundles and β-barrels routinely, though β-rich designs remain harder.

**Open questions.** One question is how sequences switch between helix and strand: metamorphic proteins such as lymphotactin and RfaH interconvert between helical and β folds. Another is how much of each helix's stability is set before folding of the full protein.

keyPoints: Secondary structure is local, regular backbone conformation held by backbone hydrogen bonds
Alpha helix: right-handed, 3.6 residues/turn, C=O of i bonds N-H of i+4
Beta sheets form from extended strands, parallel or antiparallel
Phi and psi angles, mapped on the Ramachandran plot, limit possible shapes
Proline and glycine break helices; Ala, Leu, Glu favor them
Turns and loops connect helices and strands and reverse chain direction

test.q: Which interaction mainly stabilizes alpha helices and beta sheets?
test.explain: Secondary structure is held by hydrogen bonds between backbone C=O and N-H groups. Disulfides and side-chain interactions matter more for tertiary structure.

test.q: In an alpha helix, the C=O of residue i hydrogen-bonds to the N-H of residue:
test.explain: The alpha helix uses i to i+4 bonds. An i+3 pattern is the tighter 3-10 helix, and i+5 is the pi helix.

test.q: About how many residues make one turn of an alpha helix?
test.explain: There are 3.6 residues per turn. 5.4 Å is the pitch (the rise per turn), a common mix-up.

test.q: Why does proline disrupt alpha helices?
choices: It forms disulfide bonds with neighbors
It lacks a backbone N-H and restricts phi
It carries a strong negative charge
It is too large to fit in the helix core
test.explain: Proline's ring removes the backbone N-H hydrogen-bond donor and locks the phi angle, so it breaks helices.

test.q: In a beta sheet, hydrogen bonds form mainly:
choices: Between the sheet and surrounding water
Between side chains on one face
Within one turn of a single strand
test.explain: Beta sheets are built from backbone hydrogen bonds between adjacent strands, which may lie far apart in the sequence.

test.q: Strands that run in opposite directions form which kind of sheet?
test.explain: Antiparallel sheets pair strands running in opposite directions, giving straighter hydrogen bonds than parallel sheets.

test.q: What does a Ramachandran plot show?
choices: The amino acid sequence of a protein
The charge of a protein across pH values
Allowed combinations of phi and psi angles
Rates of a reaction across substrate levels
test.explain: The plot maps phi versus psi backbone angles. Steric clashes forbid most regions, and the allowed regions match helices and sheets.

test.q: The protein in hair, keratin, is built mostly from:
test.explain: Keratin consists of long alpha helices twisted together. Silk fibroin is the classic beta-sheet example.

test.q: Which residues tend to favor beta strands?
test.explain: Beta-branched residues like valine, isoleucine and threonine favor strands. Alanine and glutamate favor helices instead.

test.q: A helix with hydrophobic residues on one face and polar residues on the other is called ___.
test.explain: Amphipathic helices can pack against a hydrophobic core or membrane with one face while the other faces water.

test.q: What four-residue structure reverses chain direction, often using glycine and proline?
test.explain: Beta turns span four residues with an i to i+3 hydrogen bond and reverse the chain.

test.q: Which scientist (with Corey and Branson) predicted the alpha helix in 1951?
test.explain: Linus Pauling, Robert Corey and Herman Branson proposed the alpha helix from model building.

kidTest.q: What does an alpha helix look like?
choices: A flat circle like a coin
kidTest.explain: An alpha helix twists like a curly spring.

kidTest.q: What does a beta sheet look like?
kidTest.explain: Beta sheets lie side by side like the folds of a pleated fan.

kidTest.q: What is a protein chain made of?
kidTest.explain: Proteins are chains of building blocks called amino acids.

kidTest.q: Why do many small sticky links matter?
choices: Together they make a strong hold
kidTest.explain: One link is weak, but lots together hold the shape firmly.

kidTest.q: The tiny sticky links are called h _ _ _ _ _ _ _ bonds.
kidTest.explain: Hydrogen bonds hold spirals and sheets in shape.

advancedTest.q: Why are short isolated peptides rarely helical even when rich in alanine?
choices: Helix nucleation has a large entropic cost before bonds pay it back
Alanine has no backbone hydrogen-bond donor
Water breaks helices faster than any stable sequence forms them
Helices form after tertiary contacts have already been set
advancedTest.explain: Zimm-Bragg theory gives a small nucleation parameter (about 10⁻³): the first turn costs entropy without forming i/i+4 bonds, so short peptides stay mostly coil.

advancedTest.q: The Minor and Kim chameleon sequence experiments imply that:
choices: Prediction accuracy is limited mainly by noisy data
Beta sheets form from residues close in sequence
Context can make one sequence form helix or strand
Local propensity alone sets secondary structure
advancedTest.explain: An identical 11-residue sequence adopted different structures in different contexts, which explains why purely local methods like Chou-Fasman plateaued.

advancedTest.q: Phosphate-binding sites often lie at helix N-termini because:
choices: The helix macrodipole leaves a partial positive end
N-terminal residues are mostly negatively charged
Hydrophobic side chains cluster at the N-terminus
Proline at N-termini forms covalent phosphate bonds
advancedTest.explain: Aligned peptide dipoles create a partial positive charge at the N-terminus, and free N-H groups there favor binding anions such as phosphate.

advancedTest.q: A peptide is helical in TFE-containing buffer by CD. The most cautious interpretation is:
choices: The native protein region is helical in vivo
The CD signal reflects a 222 nm sheet minimum
The peptide likely contains a beta-sheet core
TFE may induce helicity absent in the native context
advancedTest.explain: TFE strongly promotes helices, so helicity seen in it may not reflect the native protein. The 222 nm minimum indicates helix, not sheet.

lessons.title: Tertiary and Quaternary Structure

levels.kid:
Imagine a long necklace of beads. First, little parts of it twist into springs and zigzags. Then the whole necklace scrunches up into a ball with a very exact shape. That final ball shape is the protein's **tertiary structure**.

What holds the ball together? Beads that dislike water hide in the middle, like kids huddling under an umbrella in the rain. Beads that like water stay on the outside.

Some proteins are teams. Several balls snap together to make one bigger machine. That team shape is called **quaternary structure**. Hemoglobin, the protein that carries oxygen in your blood, is a team of four.

Shape matters a lot. If a protein's shape is wrong, it can't do its job, like a key with bent teeth.
levels.hs:
Proteins have four levels of structure. **Primary** is the amino acid sequence. **Secondary** is local folding into helices and sheets. This lesson covers the top two levels.

**Tertiary structure** is the complete 3D shape of a single polypeptide chain. It forms when helices, sheets and loops pack together. The forces that hold it include:
- **The hydrophobic effect**: nonpolar side chains (like leucine and valine) cluster in the core, away from water. This is the main driving force.
- **Hydrogen bonds** between side chains and the backbone.
- **Ionic bonds (salt bridges)** between positive and negative side chains, such as lysine and aspartate.
- **Disulfide bonds**: covalent links between two cysteine side chains, common in proteins that work outside cells.
- **Van der Waals forces** from tight packing.

**Quaternary structure** is how two or more chains (called **subunits**) fit together. Not every protein has one.

A real example: **hemoglobin** has four subunits, two alpha and two beta. When one subunit binds oxygen, it changes shape and makes the others grab oxygen more easily. Myoglobin, its muscle cousin, is a single chain with only tertiary structure.

Shape determines function. A change in one amino acid can disrupt it. In sickle cell disease, a single swap in the beta chain makes hemoglobin molecules stick together.
levels.college:
**Tertiary structure** is the full three-dimensional arrangement of every atom in one polypeptide, including side-chain positions. Most globular proteins have a nonpolar **core** and a polar, charged surface.

**Stabilizing interactions:**
- **Hydrophobic effect**: burying nonpolar side chains releases ordered water around them. The entropy gain of the water drives folding.
- **Hydrogen bonds and salt bridges**: these are individually modest. Buried ones can still add real stability.
- **Disulfide bonds**: they form between cysteines in the oxidizing ER lumen and extracellular space. They are rare in the reducing cytosol, where glutathione keeps thiols reduced.
- **Van der Waals packing**: protein cores are packed about as densely as organic crystals.
- **Metal ions and cofactors**: one example is the Zn²⁺ in zinc fingers.

**Supersecondary motifs and domains.** Recurring combinations include the helix-turn-helix, β-hairpin, βαβ unit and Greek key. A **domain** is a compact, often independently folding unit of roughly 50-250 residues. Examples are the Rossmann fold (NAD⁺ binding) and the immunoglobulin fold. Many proteins are mosaics of domains, and the same domain recurs across many proteins.

Broad classes of folds are all-α (globins), all-β (immunoglobulins), α/β (TIM barrel) and α+β.

**Quaternary structure** describes how subunits assemble. They can be identical (**homo-oligomers**, such as a homodimer) or different (**hetero-oligomers**, such as hemoglobin α₂β₂). Subunit interfaces are largely hydrophobic, with complementary shapes. Advantages include:
- **Cooperativity and allostery**, as when oxygen binding shifts hemoglobin from T to R state.
- **Genetic economy**: building large structures from repeated small genes.
- **Error reduction**: defective subunits can be replaced.
- **Bringing together active sites** or making channels (ion channel tetramers).

**Denaturation** disrupts tertiary and quaternary structure without breaking peptide bonds. It can be caused by heat, extreme pH, urea, guanidinium chloride or detergents.
levels.phd:
**Anfinsen's experiment** (ribonuclease A, 1950s-60s; Nobel 1972) showed that sequence encodes tertiary structure. RNase A was denatured in 8 M urea with β-mercaptoethanol to reduce its four disulfides. Removing both agents together restored nearly full activity. Removing urea after air-oxidizing in its presence yielded "scrambled" disulfide isomers with about 1% activity, consistent with random pairing (8 Cys give 105 possible arrangements). Trace thiol then catalyzed reshuffling to the native state. The native state is therefore thermodynamically favored under physiological conditions, the **thermodynamic hypothesis**.

**Marginal stability.** The ΔG of unfolding for typical globular proteins is only about 20-60 kJ/mol. This is the small difference between large opposing terms: favorable burial and packing versus the loss of chain conformational entropy. Stability is thus easily shifted by single mutations, which are measured as ΔΔG.

**Quantifying burial.** Kauzmann (1959) proposed the hydrophobic effect as dominant. Today, accessible surface area (Lee and Richards) correlates with folding free energy. Roughly 0.1 kJ/mol per Å² of buried nonpolar surface is a commonly cited estimate. Interior cavities from large-to-small mutations (e.g., Leu→Ala in T4 lysozyme, Matthews lab) cost stability roughly proportional to cavity volume.

**Quaternary symmetry.** Most homo-oligomers obey cyclic (Cn) or dihedral (Dn) point-group symmetry, and viral capsids use icosahedral symmetry. Caspar and Klug's quasi-equivalence explains how 60T subunits build capsids. Protein-protein interfaces typically bury about 1,200-2,000 Å² and feature **hot spots**: a few residues, often Trp, Tyr and Arg, contribute most of the binding energy (Clackson and Wells, alanine scanning).

**Hemoglobin** illustrates how quaternary structure enables function. Perutz's structures showed that O₂ binding pulls Fe²⁺ into the porphyrin plane, moving the proximal His F8. This rearranges the α1β2 interface, rotating one αβ dimer by about 15° relative to the other (T→R). The **MWC** concerted model and the **KNF** sequential model remain debated idealizations. Real hemoglobin shows features of both.

**Structure determination.** Methods include X-ray crystallography, NMR and cryo-EM, whose resolution revolution (around 2013 onward, direct electron detectors) opened up large complexes. AlphaFold2 (CASP14, 2020) now predicts many tertiary structures to near-experimental accuracy.
levels.expert:
The sequence-structure link has direct clinical consequences, and quaternary assembly is now a drug target in its own right.

**Drugging quaternary structure.**
- **Tafamidis** binds the thyroxine pockets at the dimer-dimer interface of the transthyretin (TTR) tetramer. This kinetically stabilizes the tetramer, which matters because tetramer dissociation is the rate-limiting step toward TTR amyloid cardiomyopathy and polyneuropathy. Acoramidis mimics the protective T119M variant.
- **Voxelotor** stabilized the R (oxygenated) state of HbS to reduce polymerization. It was withdrawn in 2024 after safety signals, a reminder that shifting allosteric equilibria has systemic effects, here on O₂ delivery.
- **Capsid assembly modulators** for hepatitis B misdirect core-protein oligomerization. **Lenacapavir** binds the HIV capsid hexamer interface, disrupting both assembly and nuclear import.
- **Molecular glues** such as thalidomide analogs (lenalidomide) reshape the cereblon surface to recruit neosubstrates like IKZF1/3 for degradation. This is induced quaternary structure.

**Mutations and ΔΔG.** Many missense disease variants act by destabilizing tertiary folds rather than active sites, as with many CFTR and p53 variants. In p53, Y220C creates a surface crevice now targeted by the stabilizer rezatapopt (PC14586). **Dominant-negative** effects come from oligomers: one mutant subunit poisons a tetramer, so only 1/16 of p53 tetramers are fully wild-type in a heterozygote. The same logic applies to collagen trimers in osteogenesis imperfecta.

**Neuro relevance.** Potassium channels are tetramers, and AMPA receptors assemble as dimers of dimers. Subunit composition determines properties. For example, GluA2 with its edited Q/R site renders AMPA receptors Ca²⁺-impermeable, and GABA-A pentamer composition dictates benzodiazepine sensitivity at the α/γ2 interface.

**Pitfalls and open questions.**
- **Crystal contacts versus biological interfaces.** Tools such as PISA help separate the two. Native mass spectrometry and SEC-MALS confirm stoichiometry in solution.
- **AlphaFold confidence.** High pLDDT does not guarantee the correct ligand-bound or oligomeric state. AlphaFold-Multimer and AlphaFold3 improve complexes but can hallucinate interfaces.
- **Intrinsically disordered regions.** About 30% of eukaryotic proteins contain long disordered segments, which challenges a single-structure paradigm. Many fold only upon binding.
- **Metamorphic proteins.** Proteins such as lymphotactin and KaiB switch between distinct folds, so "one sequence, one structure" is a strong tendency rather than a law.

keyPoints: Tertiary structure is the full 3D fold of one polypeptide chain
The hydrophobic effect, burying nonpolar side chains, is the main driving force
Disulfides, H-bonds, salt bridges and van der Waals packing add stability
Domains are compact, often independently folding units reused across proteins
Quaternary structure is the assembly of subunits, e.g. hemoglobin α2β2
Anfinsen showed that sequence encodes the native fold; stability is marginal

test.q: Which force is considered the main driving force of tertiary folding?
test.explain: Burying nonpolar side chains frees ordered water, and the resulting entropy gain drives folding. Peptide bonds belong to primary structure.

test.q: Quaternary structure refers to:
test.explain: Quaternary structure describes how two or more polypeptide subunits fit together.

test.q: Which protein lacks quaternary structure because it is a single chain?
test.explain: Myoglobin is a single polypeptide. Hemoglobin is α2β2, and channels and capsids are multi-subunit assemblies.

test.q: Disulfide bonds are rare in the cytosol mainly because it is:
choices: Kept too warm for stable sulfur bonding
Depleted of free cysteine by active protein synthesis
Kept too acidic for thiol groups to react
test.explain: Glutathione keeps the cytosol reducing, so cysteine thiols stay in their reduced form. Disulfides form instead in the oxidizing ER and extracellular space.

test.q: In Anfinsen's experiment, removing urea and β-mercaptoethanol together led to:
test.explain: The chain refolded into its native, active state, showing that the sequence encodes the structure.

test.q: A compact, often independently folding unit of about 50-250 residues is a:
test.explain: Domains fold on their own and are reused across proteins. Motifs are smaller recurring element combinations.

test.q: Hemoglobin's subunit composition is:
test.explain: Adult hemoglobin has two alpha and two beta subunits.

test.q: Denaturing a protein with urea typically:
test.explain: Denaturation disrupts 3D structure without cleaving the peptide backbone, so the sequence stays intact.

test.q: One advantage of quaternary structure is:
test.explain: Subunits can communicate shape changes, giving cooperativity and allostery as in hemoglobin.

test.q: Covalent links between two cysteine side chains are called ___ bonds.
test.explain: Disulfide bonds (S-S) crosslink cysteines and stabilize extracellular proteins.

test.q: What is the term for an ionic interaction between oppositely charged side chains, like lysine and aspartate?
test.explain: Salt bridges pair positive and negative side chains.

test.q: A protein made of identical subunits is called a homo-___.
test.explain: Homo-oligomers have identical subunits; hetero-oligomers have different ones.

kidTest.q: Where do the beads that dislike water go in a folded protein?
kidTest.explain: They hide inside, away from water, like kids under an umbrella.

kidTest.q: What is a protein team of several balls called?
kidTest.explain: When several folded chains join, that is quaternary structure.

kidTest.q: How many parts make up hemoglobin?
kidTest.explain: Hemoglobin is a team of four.

kidTest.q: Why does a protein's shape matter?
choices: It lets the protein do its job
kidTest.explain: Like a key, the right shape lets the protein work.

kidTest.q: Hemoglobin carries this gas in your blood: o _ _ _ _ _
kidTest.explain: Hemoglobin carries oxygen around your body.

advancedTest.q: Air-oxidizing reduced RNase A in urea, then removing urea, gave about 1% activity. Why?
choices: Disulfides formed randomly before the native fold could guide pairing
The enzyme lost its zinc cofactor during the denaturation step
Urea had cleaved peptide bonds during the oxidation step
Cysteines were chemically destroyed by prolonged air exposure
advancedTest.explain: Oxidation in the unfolded state locked in random disulfide pairings. Trace thiol was needed to reshuffle them to the native state.

advancedTest.q: A heterozygous p53 mutant subunit poisons tetramers so that only 1/16 are fully wild-type. This arises because:
choices: The mutant allele is transcribed sixteen times more often
Random mixing leaves (1/2)^4 of tetramers wild-type
Wild-type subunits are degraded faster than mutant ones
Tetramers need four mutant subunits in order to assemble
advancedTest.explain: With equal random mixing, the chance that all four subunits are wild-type is (1/2)^4 = 1/16. This is the basis of the dominant-negative effect.

advancedTest.q: Why does tafamidis help in transthyretin amyloidosis?
choices: It stabilizes the tetramer, slowing the rate-limiting dissociation
It blocks transthyretin gene transcription in the liver
It converts misfolded monomers into the native dimer form
It cleaves amyloid fibrils already deposited in heart tissue
advancedTest.explain: Tafamidis binds the thyroxine pockets at the dimer interface. This kinetically stabilizes the tetramer, preventing the dissociation that precedes amyloid formation.

advancedTest.q: A Leu→Ala core mutation destabilizes a protein by a large ΔΔG despite no change in its charge. The best explanation is:
choices: Alanine forms extra disulfides that strain the protein core
A packing cavity loses van der Waals and buried hydrophobic contacts
Alanine is too large to fit into the hydrophobic core
The peptide backbone is broken at the mutated position
advancedTest.explain: Large-to-small substitutions create cavities, and stability loss scales with cavity volume. With only marginal net stability, losing these contacts matters a great deal.

lessons.title: Folding Energy Landscapes and Molecular Chaperones

levels.kid:
Imagine a ball rolling down a big bumpy hill. It wobbles, gets stuck in little dips, then rolls on until it reaches the very bottom. A new protein does something like that. It starts as a long floppy string and folds itself into one special shape, the shape with the lowest energy.

Inside a cell, though, it is very crowded. A half-folded protein might stick to its neighbors in a messy clump.

So cells have helpers called **chaperones**. Like a grown-up at a school dance, they keep proteins from grabbing the wrong partner. Some chaperones even give a protein its own quiet little room to fold in. They use energy from a fuel molecule called ATP to do their job.
levels.hs:
A protein's amino acid sequence contains the information needed to reach its final 3D shape, called the **native state**. In the 1950s and 60s, Christian Anfinsen showed this with the enzyme ribonuclease. He unfolded it with chemicals, then removed them, and it refolded and worked again. This idea is called **Anfinsen's dogma**.

But how does a chain find the right shape so fast? Testing every possible shape would take longer than the age of the universe. This puzzle is **Levinthal's paradox**. The answer is the **energy landscape**, often drawn as a **folding funnel**. Unfolded chains sit at the wide, high-energy top. As they form helpful contacts, especially by burying water-fearing (hydrophobic) side chains, they slide downhill toward the native state at the narrow bottom. Small dips along the way are **kinetic traps**, wrong shapes where a chain can get stuck.

In the crowded cell, partly folded proteins expose sticky hydrophobic patches that can clump together. **Molecular chaperones** prevent this. They do not encode the final shape. They help proteins avoid wrong turns.

A real example: **heat shock proteins** (Hsps) are chaperones made in larger amounts when cells get hot. Heat unfolds proteins, so cells need more helpers. Hsp70 grabs exposed sticky segments, and the GroEL/GroES complex in bacteria acts like a folding chamber.
levels.college:
**Thermodynamics.** The native state is usually only marginally stable: the free energy of unfolding (ΔG) is typically about 20 to 60 kJ/mol. That margin is the small difference between large opposing terms:
- Favorable: the **hydrophobic effect** (releasing ordered water from nonpolar surfaces), van der Waals packing, hydrogen bonds and salt bridges.
- Unfavorable: loss of **conformational entropy** of the chain.

**The funnel.** Levinthal's paradox goes away if folding is a biased search, not a random one. A rugged funnel means the chain moves through many routes. Many small proteins fold in a **two-state** way, with no populated intermediates, in microseconds to milliseconds. Larger proteins often pass through a **molten globule**: compact, with secondary structure but loosely packed side chains.

**Chaperone families:**
- **Hsp70** (DnaK in *E. coli*): binds short hydrophobic stretches. In the ATP state it has low affinity and fast exchange. ATP hydrolysis, stimulated by **Hsp40/J-domain** cochaperones, locks the lid closed with high affinity. Nucleotide exchange factors (GrpE) then reset it. Repeated cycles of binding and release keep proteins from aggregating.
- **Chaperonins**: group I (**GroEL/GroES**) are two stacked 7-subunit rings. A substrate binds the hydrophobic rim, GroES caps the ring, and the cavity wall turns hydrophilic. The protein then folds alone in this "Anfinsen cage" for roughly 10 seconds, timed by ATP hydrolysis. Group II (**TRiC/CCT** in eukaryotes) uses a built-in lid and folds actin and tubulin.
- **Hsp90**: works late in folding to mature "client" proteins such as steroid hormone receptors and many kinases.
- **Small Hsps**: ATP-independent "holdases" that buffer unfolded proteins during stress.

Chaperones speed up proper yield, not the folding chemistry itself. Some steps are also sped up by **enzymes**: protein disulfide isomerase and peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerases.
levels.phd:
**Landscape theory.** Bryngelson and Wolynes formalized folding via the **principle of minimal frustration**: evolved sequences have native interactions that are mutually consistent. The landscape's gradient toward the native state (stability gap, δE) is large relative to its roughness (ΔE), so the folding temperature exceeds the glass transition temperature (Tf/Tg > 1). Random sequences lack this and get trapped in glassy states. Onuchic, Wolynes and Dill popularized the funnel picture.

**Kinetics.** Fersht's **phi-value analysis** compares the destabilizing effect of mutations on the transition state and on the native state. Φ ≈ 1 means a residue is structured in the transition state; Φ ≈ 0 means unstructured, revealing a **nucleation-condensation** mechanism. Plaxco, Simons and Baker showed two-state folding rates correlate with **contact order** (average sequence separation of contacting residues), so topology, more than size, sets the speed. Chevron plots of log k versus denaturant give m-values that report burial of surface area in the transition state.

**Chaperone mechanism.** Hsp70 allostery couples the nucleotide-binding domain to the substrate-binding domain's β-sandwich and α-helical lid. Hsp70 may act as an unfoldase as well as a holdase, pulling misfolded species back up the landscape (entropic pulling). For GroEL there is a debate: the **passive cage** model says confinement only blocks aggregation, while the **active** model says the cavity's confinement and net negative charge smooth the landscape and speed folding of some substrates such as DM-MBP (Hartl group). Iterative annealing (Thirumalai and Lorimer) proposes repeated forced unfolding by ring binding. GroEL holds substrates up to about 60 kDa, and about 10% of *E. coli* proteins interact with it, with roughly 85 being obligate clients (Kerner et al., 2005).

**Cotranslational folding.** Domains can fold in the ribosome exit tunnel vestibule. Trigger factor (bacteria) and NAC/RAC (eukaryotes) engage nascent chains, and codon-dependent translation pauses may give domains time to fold.

**Proteostasis.** Balch, Morimoto, Dillin and Kelly framed the **proteostasis network**: synthesis, chaperone folding and degradation as an adaptable system. **HSF1** drives heat shock protein expression when chaperones are diverted to misfolded proteins.
levels.expert:
**Pharmacology of folding.** Chaperones and folding are drug targets:
- **Pharmacological chaperones** bind and stabilize a mutant protein's native state, shifting the equilibrium. **Tafamidis** stabilizes the transthyretin tetramer in transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy. **Migalastat** stabilizes amenable mutant α-galactosidase A in Fabry disease, a small-molecule trick with an enzyme's own inhibitor.
- **CFTR correctors**: the common ΔF508 mutation misfolds the NBD1 domain, and the ER quality-control system destroys it. **Elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor** combines correctors (folding and trafficking rescue) with a potentiator (channel opening), a landmark of folding-directed therapy.
- **Hsp90 inhibitors** (geldanamycin derivatives, ganetespib) aimed to degrade oncogenic client kinases. Most trials disappointed because of toxicity and HSF1-driven compensatory upregulation of Hsp70, but **pimitespib** gained approval in Japan for GIST.

**Neurosurgical and neurological relevance.** Neurons cannot dilute misfolded protein by dividing, and chaperone capacity declines with age. Hsp70 and the Hsp110/DNAJB1 disaggregase system can disassemble α-synuclein fibrils in vitro, but it might also create seeds that spread. Raising chaperone activity is therefore not uniformly protective. Proteostasis also matters in brain tumors, where cancer cells "addict" themselves to Hsp90 and HSF1.

**Evolution.** Chaperones **buffer mutations**: Rutherford and Lindquist showed that reducing Hsp90 in *Drosophila* revealed hidden morphological variation. Chaperones thus let destabilizing yet potentially useful mutations persist.

**Computation.** **AlphaFold2** (2020-21) predicts static native structures with near-experimental accuracy for many domains, but it does not simulate folding pathways, kinetic traps or chaperone dependence. Long molecular dynamics runs on the Anton supercomputer (Shaw group, 2011) folded fast-folding mini-proteins and largely confirmed funnel ideas.

**Pitfalls and open questions.** In vitro refolding at low concentration overstates how independent folding is in the cell. Thermal stability (Tm) is not the same as kinetic stability. It is still unclear how much of the proteome strictly needs chaperones and how the ribosome shapes folding pathways. Single-molecule force spectroscopy and in-cell NMR are starting to give answers.

keyPoints: Anfinsen: the amino acid sequence encodes the native 3D structure
Levinthal's paradox: a random search for the native shape would take far too long
A funnel-shaped energy landscape biases folding downhill, with kinetic traps along the way
Native proteins are only marginally stable, driven mainly by the hydrophobic effect
Chaperones (Hsp70, GroEL/GroES, TRiC, Hsp90) prevent aggregation, often using ATP
Pharmacological chaperones and CFTR correctors treat folding diseases

test.q: What did Anfinsen's ribonuclease experiment show?
choices: Unfolded enzymes stay inactive after cleanup
The amino acid sequence encodes the native shape
Chaperones encode the final protein shape
test.explain: Denatured ribonuclease refolded and regained activity once the chemicals were removed, so the sequence carries the folding information.

test.q: Levinthal's paradox points out that:
choices: Folding requires much more energy than cells have
A random search of shapes would take far too long
Proteins fold too slowly to support life
Hydrophobic residues prefer the protein surface
test.explain: Testing every conformation would take longer than the age of the universe, yet proteins fold in milliseconds. Biased landscapes explain this.

test.q: In the folding funnel, the narrow bottom represents:
test.explain: The native state sits at the lowest free energy, at the narrow bottom. Unfolded chains start at the wide top.

test.q: What is the main driving force of protein folding?
test.explain: Burying nonpolar side chains frees ordered water. Chain entropy is actually lost during folding, which opposes it.

test.q: How does the GroEL/GroES complex help a protein fold?
choices: It adds sugar groups to sticky regions
It cuts the protein into smaller domains
It encloses the protein in a protected chamber
test.explain: GroES caps the GroEL ring, forming an "Anfinsen cage" with a hydrophilic wall where the protein folds alone.

test.q: Hsp70 recognizes misfolded or new proteins mainly by binding:
test.explain: Hsp70 binds short hydrophobic segments that would normally be buried, which prevents them from clumping.

test.q: Why do cells make more heat shock proteins when warmed?
choices: Heat destroys the cell's ATP reserves
Heat slows down new protein synthesis
Heat makes most proteins more stable
test.explain: Heat unfolds proteins and exposes sticky patches, so more chaperones are needed. HSF1 drives this response.

test.q: A compact folding intermediate with secondary structure but loose side-chain packing is called a:
test.explain: The molten globule is compact and has secondary structure but lacks the tight packing of the native state.

test.q: Which chaperone matures client proteins such as steroid receptors and kinases?
test.explain: Hsp90 works late in folding to mature specific clients. Its kinase clients made it a cancer drug target.

test.q: A wrong low-energy dip where a folding chain gets stuck is called a kinetic ___.
test.explain: Kinetic traps are misfolded local minima on a rugged energy landscape.

test.q: What is the general name for proteins that help other proteins fold without dictating their final shape?
test.explain: Molecular chaperones prevent wrong interactions. The sequence still encodes the final shape.

test.q: Most chaperones like Hsp70 and GroEL power their cycles by hydrolyzing ___.
test.explain: ATP binding and hydrolysis switch these chaperones between low- and high-affinity states.

kidTest.q: What does a new protein start out as?
kidTest.explain: A new protein is a chain that folds into its special shape.

kidTest.q: Folding is like a ball doing what?
kidTest.explain: The protein goes "downhill" to its lowest-energy shape.

kidTest.q: What can happen to half-folded proteins in a crowded cell?
kidTest.explain: Sticky parts can make proteins clump with their neighbors.

kidTest.q: What fuel do chaperones use?
kidTest.explain: ATP is the cell's energy molecule.

kidTest.q: Helper proteins that keep folding proteins from clumping are called c _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Chaperones are like a grown-up at a dance, keeping proteins from grabbing the wrong partner.

advancedTest.q: Folding rates of two-state proteins correlate best with contact order. This suggests that folding speed is set mainly by:
choices: Total molecular weight of the chain
Overall net charge at physiological pH
The number of disulfide bonds present
The topology of the native fold
advancedTest.explain: Plaxco, Simons and Baker found that topology, more than size, predicts the rate. Proteins dominated by local contacts fold faster.

advancedTest.q: A mutation destabilizes the native state by 4 kJ/mol and the transition state by about 0.2 kJ/mol. What does the phi value imply about this residue?
choices: It stabilizes the unfolded state over the native one
It is fully structured in the transition state
It forms a nucleus that limits the folding rate
It is largely unstructured in the transition state
advancedTest.explain: Φ ≈ 0.05, near zero, means the residue's native contacts have not formed yet when the transition state is reached.

advancedTest.q: Why might Hsp90 inhibitors have underperformed in cancer trials, despite degrading oncogenic clients?
choices: Freeing HSF1 boosts compensatory Hsp70 levels
They block ATP synthesis in the mitochondria
They promote GroEL expression in tumor cells
Client kinases fold correctly without Hsp90 help
advancedTest.explain: Hsp90 inhibition releases HSF1, which raises Hsp70 and other protective chaperones. Toxicity also limited these drugs.

advancedTest.q: Under the minimal-frustration principle, what separates evolved sequences from random ones?
choices: Strict dependence on chaperonins to reach the native state
A higher overall content of hydrophobic residues
A larger number of populated folding intermediates
A large stability gap relative to landscape roughness
advancedTest.explain: Evolved sequences have consistent native interactions, so Tf exceeds Tg. Random sequences get stuck in glassy, frustrated states.

lessons.title: Misfolding and Aggregation: Amyloid and Prions

levels.kid:
Proteins are tiny machines in your body. Each one has to fold into just the right shape, like folding paper into a paper crane.

Sometimes a protein folds the wrong way. A wrongly folded protein can be sticky. Sticky proteins clump together with other sticky proteins, like wet sand forming lumps.

Some clumps grow into long, strong strings called **amyloid**. In the brain, these clumps can slowly hurt nerve cells. That happens in an illness called Alzheimer's disease.

There is a very strange kind of misfolded protein called a **prion**. A prion can push normal proteins to fold the wrong way too, like one bad apple spoiling the whole basket. Scientists study these clumps so they can find ways to stop them.
levels.hs:
A protein works only when it folds into its correct 3D shape, called its **native state**. **Misfolding** happens when a protein takes on a wrong shape. Misfolded proteins often expose **hydrophobic** (water-avoiding) parts that are normally tucked inside. Those greasy patches stick to each other, so the proteins **aggregate**, or clump.

One especially stable kind of clump is **amyloid**. Amyloid fibrils are long, thin fibers built from many copies of a protein. The copies are stacked into **beta sheets** that run across the fiber like the rungs of a ladder. This arrangement is called the **cross-beta** structure. Amyloid is very hard for cells to break down.

Amyloid and related clumps appear in several brain diseases:
- **Alzheimer's disease**: amyloid-beta plaques and tau tangles
- **Parkinson's disease**: alpha-synuclein clumps called Lewy bodies
- **Huntington's disease**: huntingtin protein with too many glutamines

**Prions** are misfolded proteins that can spread. The misfolded form, PrPSc, acts as a template that converts the normal protein, PrPC, into more PrPSc. Because of this, prion diseases can even be transmitted between animals and people. Examples are **Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease** (CJD) in humans and "mad cow disease" (BSE) in cattle. Stanley Prusiner won the 1997 Nobel Prize for discovering prions.
levels.college:
Folding competes with **aggregation**. Partially folded intermediates expose hydrophobic surfaces and backbone hydrogen-bonding groups. Normally chaperones and degradation pathways (ubiquitin-proteasome, autophagy) handle them. When that quality control is overwhelmed, molecules associate into amorphous aggregates, oligomers, or ordered **amyloid fibrils**.

**Amyloid features:**
- **Cross-beta** architecture: beta strands lie perpendicular to the fibril axis. X-ray fiber diffraction shows reflections at about 4.7 Å (strand spacing) and about 10 Å (sheet spacing).
- Binds the dyes **Congo red** (apple-green birefringence under polarized light) and **thioflavin T** (fluorescence).
- Many unrelated sequences can form it, so amyloid reflects a generic backbone conformation.

**Nucleation-dependent polymerization.** Fibril formation shows a lag phase, a rapid growth phase, and a plateau. Making the first nucleus is unfavorable. After that, monomers add quickly to the ends of the fibril. Adding preformed "seeds" removes the lag phase. **Secondary nucleation** on fibril surfaces speeds up the process.

**Disease examples:**
- Alzheimer's: Aβ42 (from APP cleavage by β- and γ-secretase) and hyperphosphorylated **tau**
- Parkinson's: **α-synuclein**
- Huntington's: polyglutamine expansion (CAG repeats, disease at roughly 36 or more)
- Systemic: transthyretin (ATTR) and light-chain (AL) amyloidosis deposit in the heart, nerves and kidneys

**Prions.** PrPC is a mostly α-helical GPI-anchored membrane protein. PrPSc is β-rich, partly protease-resistant and self-templating. The *PRNP* codon 129 polymorphism (Met/Val) affects susceptibility. Prion diseases include sporadic, familial and acquired CJD, variant CJD (linked to BSE), fatal familial insomnia, and kuru.
levels.phd:
Dobson argued that amyloid is a thermodynamically accessible state of most polypeptides. The backbone hydrogen-bonded cross-β spine can, in some cases, be more stable than the native fold at high concentration. Native folds persist because of kinetic barriers and cellular **proteostasis**. In this view, disease reflects concentration, mutation, aging and declining quality control rather than unique sequences.

**Structure.** Eisenberg's microcrystal structures revealed the **steric zipper**: paired β-sheets with interdigitating side chains forming a dry interface. Cryo-EM has since solved patient-derived fibrils. Fitzpatrick, Scheres and Goedert (2017) showed that tau filaments from Alzheimer's brain differ from those in Pick's disease, CTE and CBD. One sequence can adopt multiple **polymorphs**, and each fold correlates with a distinct disease. This mirrors prion **strains**, which keep heritable conformations with distinct incubation times and lesion patterns.

**Kinetics.** Knowles and colleagues developed master equations fitting thioflavin T curves. They showed that for Aβ42, fibril-catalyzed secondary nucleation dominates oligomer production once fibrils exist.

**Toxic species.** Soluble oligomers, not mature fibrils, may be the main toxic agents. Proposed mechanisms include membrane permeabilization, synaptic dysfunction and sequestration of essential proteins. Plaque burden correlates poorly with cognition, whereas tau tangle spread tracks symptoms (Braak staging).

**Prion proof.** The protein-only hypothesis gained strong support from several findings. *Prnp*-knockout mice resist infection (Büeler, Weissmann, 1993). Recombinant PrP fibrils propagated in vitro can cause disease (Legname, Prusiner, 2004; Wang, Ma, 2010, with cofactors). Codon 129 heterozygosity protects, which fits the idea that matched sequences template more efficiently. Prion-like cell-to-cell spread has also been shown for α-synuclein and tau (Luk, Lee, 2012). Whether these proteins are truly infectious between people is contested, apart from iatrogenic Aβ transmission after cadaveric growth hormone (Jaunmuktane, 2015; Banerjee, 2024).

Not all amyloid is pathological. **Functional amyloids** include Pmel17 in melanosomes, bacterial curli, and yeast [PSI+].
levels.expert:
**Diagnostics.** The **RT-QuIC** assay detects prion seeding in CSF or skin with specificity near 100%. It has largely replaced 14-3-3 testing and supports MRI (cortical ribboning, caudate/putamen DWI hyperintensity) in diagnosing sporadic CJD. α-Synuclein seed amplification assays (SAA) now detect synucleinopathy in CSF before motor symptoms. They anchor proposed biological definitions of Parkinson's disease, such as the SynNeurGe and NSD-ISS frameworks. Plasma p-tau217 has emerged as a highly accurate blood marker of Alzheimer's pathology. Amyloid and tau PET allow staging in living patients.

**Therapies targeting Aβ.** Anti-Aβ antibodies **lecanemab** (protofibril-preferring) and **donanemab** (targets pyroglutamate-modified plaque Aβ) slowed decline by roughly 27–35% over 18 months in phase 3 trials (CLARITY AD, TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2). The benefit is modest, and the clinical meaning of it is debated. **ARIA** (amyloid-related imaging abnormalities: edema or microhemorrhage) is the key risk. APOE ε4 homozygotes have the highest risk, so genotyping and MRI monitoring are required. Aducanumab's controversial approval and withdrawal remains a cautionary tale about surrogate endpoints.

**Systemic amyloidosis wins.** **Tafamidis** binds the thyroxine site of the transthyretin tetramer and blocks the rate-limiting dissociation into monomers. It is a landmark example of kinetic stabilization by small molecules (Kelly lab). TTR silencers include siRNA (patisiran, vutrisiran) and antisense drugs. In-vivo CRISPR knockdown (NTLA-2001) cut serum TTR by about 90%. AL amyloidosis is treated by eliminating the plasma-cell clone that makes the light chain.

**Neurosurgical relevance.** Prions resist standard autoclaving and formaldehyde, which makes them an infection-control hazard. Iatrogenic CJD followed dura mater grafts, depth electrodes, corneal transplants and pituitary hormone. Suspected cases require quarantined instruments or extended steam sterilization with sodium hydroxide protocols. Cerebral amyloid angiopathy causes lobar hemorrhages and affects the risk of anticoagulation and surgery.

**Open questions.** Key unknowns include which species is toxic, why particular neurons are vulnerable, and whether strain-specific therapies are needed. Others are whether tau-directed or ASO approaches (for example, tominersen for Huntington's) can succeed, and how co-pathologies (TDP-43, LATE) blunt single-target drugs.

keyPoints: Misfolded proteins expose hydrophobic surfaces and aggregate
Amyloid fibrils have a cross-beta structure and bind Congo red and thioflavin T
Fibril formation is nucleation-dependent; seeds abolish the lag phase
Alzheimer's (Aβ, tau), Parkinson's (α-synuclein), Huntington's (polyQ) involve aggregation
Prions (PrPSc) template misfolding of normal PrPC and are transmissible
RT-QuIC, anti-Aβ antibodies and TTR stabilizers turn this science into medicine

test.q: Why do misfolded proteins tend to clump together?
choices: They are coated by too many water molecules
They gain extra disulfide bonds to the membrane
Their buried hydrophobic patches become exposed
Their peptide bonds break into free amino acids
test.explain: Misfolding exposes greasy surfaces that are normally buried, and these surfaces stick to each other. Peptide bonds stay intact during misfolding.

test.q: In the cross-beta structure of amyloid, the beta strands run:
test.explain: The strands stack like ladder rungs across the fiber axis. This produces the 4.7 Å reflection in X-ray diffraction.

test.q: Which dye gives apple-green birefringence when it binds amyloid?
test.explain: Congo red-stained amyloid shows apple-green birefringence under polarized light. Thioflavin T fluoresces instead.

test.q: Adding preformed fibril seeds to a solution of monomers mainly:
test.explain: The lag phase reflects slow nucleation. Seeds bypass that step, so growth starts right away.

test.q: Lewy bodies in Parkinson's disease are built mainly from:
test.explain: Alpha-synuclein aggregates form Lewy bodies. Amyloid-beta forms Alzheimer's plaques.

test.q: How does PrPSc differ from PrPC?
choices: It is mostly alpha-helical and easily digested
It is a nucleic acid made by a virus
It is rich in beta sheet and resists proteases
It has a different amino acid sequence
test.explain: PrPSc has the same sequence as PrPC but a different, beta-rich shape. That shape is partly protease-resistant and acts as a template.

test.q: Huntington's disease aggregation is caused by expansion of:
test.explain: Expanded CAG repeats encode long polyglutamine tracts in huntingtin, and these tracts drive aggregation.

test.q: Which enzymes cut APP to release amyloid-beta?
test.explain: Sequential cleavage by β-secretase and then γ-secretase releases Aβ peptides such as Aβ42.

test.q: Which human illness is a prion disease?
test.explain: CJD is caused by prions. The others involve autoimmunity or other mechanisms.

test.q: Who won the 1997 Nobel Prize for discovering prions?
test.explain: Stanley Prusiner proposed and characterized prions as infectious proteins.

test.q: Long fibers of stacked beta sheets formed by misfolded proteins are called ___ fibrils.
test.explain: Amyloid fibrils share the cross-beta architecture.

test.q: In Alzheimer's disease, hyperphosphorylated ___ forms neurofibrillary tangles.
test.explain: Tau tangles accompany Aβ plaques, and their spread tracks with symptoms.

kidTest.q: What can happen when a protein folds the wrong way?
kidTest.explain: Wrongly folded proteins can be sticky and clump together.

kidTest.q: What are long strings of clumped proteins called?
kidTest.explain: Amyloid is the name for those long, strong protein strings.

kidTest.q: What does a prion do to normal proteins?
choices: It makes them fold wrong too
kidTest.explain: A prion spreads its wrong shape, like one bad apple spoiling the basket.

kidTest.q: Which illness has protein clumps in the brain?
kidTest.explain: Alzheimer's disease involves amyloid clumps that hurt nerve cells.

kidTest.q: A misfolded protein that spreads its bad shape is a p _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Prions push normal proteins into the wrong shape.

advancedTest.q: Tau filaments from Alzheimer's and Pick's disease have the same sequence but different cryo-EM folds. This best supports:
choices: Conformational polymorphs behave like prion strains
Disease phenotype depends on point mutations in tau
Fibrils are artifacts of sample preparation
advancedTest.explain: One sequence adopting distinct, disease-specific folds mirrors heritable prion strains. Mutations are not needed for these differences.

advancedTest.q: Why does Dobson's view predict that many unrelated proteins can form amyloid?
choices: Most sequences share a conserved amyloid motif
Amyloid forms solely from glutamine-rich domains
The cross-beta spine relies on backbone hydrogen bonds
Chaperones actively convert natives into fibrils
advancedTest.explain: Because backbone hydrogen bonds are common to all polypeptides, amyloid is a generic accessible state rather than a sequence-specific fold.

advancedTest.q: Tafamidis works in transthyretin amyloidosis by:
choices: Silencing TTR mRNA in the liver
Killing the clone that secretes TTR
advancedTest.explain: Tetramer dissociation is rate-limiting. Binding the thyroxine site stabilizes the tetramer kinetically. siRNA drugs are what silence the mRNA.

advancedTest.q: Plaque burden correlates poorly with cognition, yet blocking secondary nucleation is still attractive. Why?
choices: Fibril surfaces catalyze production of toxic oligomers
It is the step that consumes most monomer
Inhibiting it removes tau tangles directly
Secondary nucleation forms plaques without oligomers
advancedTest.explain: Knowles' kinetics show that fibril-catalyzed secondary nucleation dominates oligomer generation, and oligomers may be the main toxic species. Most monomer is consumed by elongation at fibril ends, not by secondary nucleation.
